name: miluk tɬiis
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Douglas-Tavani, Jordan A.G. 2024. A Reference Grammar of miluk tɬiis: tɬə miluk tɬiis buuqw. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara (chair M. Mithun; committee M. Gordon, J. Pérez González, S. Gildea). Open access:https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5rh4w59v
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.3 'Stress' pp. 60-68; placement statement §2.3.2 'Placement of Stress' pp. 63-64, exx. 2.31-2.34; connected-speech pattern, deviations and clitics pp. 65-68 (exx. 2.35-2.47).
catalog_quote: The placement of stress (tɬə ɬinnwi k’ellis də gila’is) in miluk has not been previously described. As with many, if not most languages with stress systems, there are tendencies but with many exceptions. Stress tends to be assigned to the penultimate syllable in a word, as in (2.31) and (2.32). ... This analysis of penultimate stress is complicated by how Jacobs often marked stress on multiple syllables within the same word, especially in connected speech, as in (2.33) and (2.34). ... This is indicative of a secondary-stress system. Specifically, primary stress appears to go on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stresses branching leftward in what typically appear to be trochaic feet, as in (2.33) and (2.34) above. The acoustic differences between primary and secondary stress are not known due to the limitations of the primary sources. ... Stress still appears to be primarily on the penultimate syllable in a word, with left-branching trochees thereafter, as in (2.36) – (2.39). This rhythmic pattern appears to include clitics (e.g. (2.36) with =iɬ; (2.37) with tɬə=), suggesting that clitics are part of the prosodic word. ... Ultimately, it is unclear at present why deviations from this general stress placement pattern occur.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of the word (e.g. híich’i 'one', pxwáanis 'bruise', adzú’an 'eight', pəxáawəl, mich’lé’wəs), based on Jacobs' acute-accent markings in elicited words and texts; the author presents it as a tendency with many unexplained exceptions, not an exceptionless rule. Main acoustic correlate is duration (Douglas-Tavani & Shirtz n.d.); Jacobs 1939:18 described stressed syllables as higher-pitched (level or falling) and longer.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses branch leftward from the penult in trochaic feet (e.g. gyínwuts’úwa, híchhijínai); acoustic difference between primary and secondary not determinable from the archival sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Many deviations in connected speech (exx. 2.40-2.43) left unexplained; words with every syllable marked stressed attributed to storytelling/phrase-level prominence (2.35); clitics are inside the prosodic word for the trochaic count but are dispreferred as stress hosts even when penultimate (2.44-2.45), though they can bear stress, especially in 'symbiotic clitic clusters' (2.46-2.47); enclitic =wu interacts with stress assignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement; evidence is Jacobs' 1930s transcriptions of Annie Miner Peterson (isolated elicited words, ex. 2.31, and connected text, ex. 2.32ff) plus one phonograph recording; author notes sentence-phrase (intonation-unit) level pressures likely influence stress marks in texts. Language is dormant; description is archival-philological.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes miluk tɬiis (Miluk, Lower Coquille; glottocode milu1241, ISO iml) as recorded almost entirely from one speaker, Annie Miner Peterson, by Melville Jacobs in 1933-34; not Hanis Coos (coos1249), which the author treats as a separate language (hanis tɬii'iis).

new_statements.quote: Higher tone, varying from a third to an octave and subject to rhetorical factors, is integral with stress-accent. In Miluk the stressed long vowel usually takes a high-to-level or high-falling tone. In Hanis the stressed element of double length does not always fall in tone but may remain high until completion of the syllable. Short stressed elements take high tone in both dialects. Special tonal indications to distinguish Hanis from Miluk were not made because tonal behavior is regularly as described and contingent upon the primary factor of stress. [...] the problem of syllable stress in both dialects [...] provided a harrassing network of matters that made the earlier recordings difficult and the results sometimes variable.
new_statements.citation: Jacobs, Melville. 1939. Coos narrative and ethnologic texts. University of Washington Publications in Anthropology 8(1):1-126. Seattle: University of Washington. ('Phonetics', pp. 13-18; stress-accent p. 18)
new_statements.locator: 'Phonetics', printed p. 18 (p. 22 of the copy consulted; lines ~851-857) for the stress-accent/tone paragraph and the 'problem of syllable stress' remark; printed pp. 17-18 (pp. 21-22) for accented CVC syllables with sonorant codas; printed p. 16 (p. 20) 'Prosodic emphasis in Coos is upon a proper weighting of syllables'.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Douglas-Tavani 2024: penultimate tendency, 'not previously described'): Jacobs 1939 is silent on WHERE stress falls and himself calls syllable stress an unsolved problem, which is exactly why Douglas-Tavani could say placement was undescribed. What it adds: the type of system (stress-accent with pitch contingent on stress, i.e. not a tone language; Miluk stressed long vowels take high-level/high-falling pitch), sonorant-coda lengthening under accent, and vowel reduction in unaccented final syllables. No contradiction; no independent confirmation of penult placement either. The bib_tag 'likely states stress' is only half right: it states stress exists and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jacobs treats Coos (both Hanis and Miluk) as a stress-accent language: stress is the 'primary factor' and pitch is a predictable correlate of it (Miluk stressed long vowels high-level or high-falling, short stressed vowels high, in both dialects), so tone is not contrastive. He marks stress in the texts (acute after the vowel, e.g. M. li'nwi 'strong') but gives NO rule for which syllable carries it; he explicitly lists 'the problem of syllable stress in both dialects' among matters left for a later grammatical treatment. He also notes that an accented CVC syllable closed by n, m, l tends to be made heavy by lengthening the sonorant (non-phonemic), and that 'prosodic emphasis in Coos is upon a proper weighting of syllables'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. (Douglas-Tavani 2024 observes that Jacobs's texts often mark stress on more than one syllable of a word, but Jacobs 1939 itself does not discuss this.)
new_statements.exceptions: None as to placement (no placement rule is given). Notes: unaccented final CVC/VC syllables have reduced (dulled) vowels (printed p. 14); more than one raised period marks emphatic over-lengthening (he-'--niye 'long long ago').
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs 1939 treats both Coos languages together as 'two Coos dialects', Hanis (H.) and Miluk (M.), from Mrs. Annie Miner Peterson (1933-34); the Miluk-specific sentence is 'In Miluk the stressed long vowel usually takes a high-to-level or high-falling tone'. the copy consulted sits in the Hanis folder (coos1249) because the same pages serve both languages; a pointer was added to milu1241/.
